posts.text: The Zuck has released Muse Wonder 🦎

Two more interesting insights that was probably drowned in the release news:

Meta built Wonder for agents that act on your behalf, starting with its Muse app. Two features are really important: active memory, which keeps track of what matters to you across conversations, and active focus, which keeps a task going when it gets hard, tries other approaches and recovers from errors. 

Wang says Meta invested in memory "disproportionately" compared with other labs. The models were trained on Meta's Prometheus cluster in Ohio, with large-scale pre-training followed by reinforcement learning, after Zuckerberg had already committed a capital budget of $100 billion or more.

Active memory and active focus make Meta Muse even more exciting, because they allow for much more accurate and comprehensive execution of essential tasks.

(P.S.: Can we *please* finally get Meta Muse in Europe too?!)

Anthropic says new safeguards have cut the distillation that rival labs can pull out of Claude by 10 to 100 times ("around 90 to 99 percent"). 

Anthropic names Chinese labs Zhipu and Moonshot, and says one network once ran more than 20,000 fake accounts at a time.

It remains to be seen whether GLM and Kimi will continue to release outstanding models when they can barely distill anymore.

Meta may have a major consumer AI success on its hands with Muse.

Now its getting interesting! Microsoft is taking on Nvidia in AI inference with a multi-gigawatt expansion of its own chips.

Starting in 2027, Microsoft plans to make Azure Maia the primary inference system for its own products and services.

Maia 200 already serves production workloads including Microsoft Copilot, running OpenAI models, Microsoft's own MAI models and open-source models.

Maia 300 begins production deployments in 2027. Microsoft expects it to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.

Microsoft does not name Nvidia in the announcement, but the planned rollout could reduce its reliance on Nvidia GPUs for running its own AI services massively.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team believes small AI models may now be months away from being capable of self replicating without access to a datacenter.

Quoting from the blog:

'The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).

At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.'
